# Copper March 2011 

- Natural disasters such as Cyclone Yasi in February and the Japanese earthquake-tsunami earlier this month would typically bring the type of uncertainty in commodities markets which prompts prices higher out of supply concern. The immediate market reaction on March 15th – the day the tsunami images were everywhere – was to sell copper, and it fell by $235/t as the general consensus was that Japan will be, for the near-term, a metal consumer of dwindling importance.  Yet within a day, copper had picked itself up, and the month’s second half cash average price of US$9550/t ($4.33/lb) mirrored the first. 

- Slight revisions to our supply side for 2011 since our last report (up 100kt) have reduced our overall market deficit for 2011 to just under the 0.5Mt mark, but we have largely kept our price forecasts in place because of our belief that China will come back in the second quarter with significant interest in the metal. 

- With winter now officially behind us, the warmer spring air is refreshing spirits, although to say that global demand has spring in its step would be an exaggeration.  While activity in Europe has maintained its solid pace of last year, the same cannot be said of the key market China, with semis production lower in the first few months of 2011. Activity in the US is a little better and while Japan also got off to a steady start, clearly there are short term troubles ahead for the country. 

- The tragic events in Japan, and subsequent suspension of operations at three copper metallurgical operations and the ongoing closure of the Onahama smelter/refinery is releasing (or at least displacing) ~60kt/m of copper concentrates into the Asian custom smelting market.  As a consequence, there has been a material uplift in spot TC/RCs during the second half of March with rates having more than doubled from $55/t & 5.5c/lb last month, to $110-120/t & 11-12c/lb currently.

## Market Developments

conomic stability has again come under question. Ratings agency Standard & Poor’s downgraded both Portugal and Greece late this month following a new debt rescue system agreed at an EU summit. In the USA, the negative news on higher consumer prices and a housing sector that continues to struggle outweighed more optimistic data from earlier in the month on industrial production gains. **..and rising stocks…** We have also noted in previous reports how LME copper stocks have risen month on month since November, and this month was no exception. Ending February at 423kt, stocks across LME warehouses now stand at almost 440kt. Comex stocks have remained more or less constant, fluctuating in a narrow range of 75-77kt over the course of this month. And Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks rose substantially from end-February’s 134.3kt to 172.2kt on March 29th , although this did take in c.30kt from two bonded warehouses (Tongshen Yangshan and Zhongchu Lin Gang) which had not been included before. **..can be offset by mine losses…** Ordinarily, rising stocks can often be countered during the month by reports of various mine or plant outages for reasons of strike action or weather-related events. We lost 835kt copper in mine feed this way last year, and 960kt the year before. But in March events such as these were few and far between. On Thursday March 24th , 600 workers at the Chambishi smelter in Zambia, owned by China Non-Ferrous Metals Corp and Yunnan Copper Industry, struck over pay issues. But this lasted until the 26th o

nly, when both work and pay negotiations both resumed. Codelco also noted production problems at Gaby that we estimate may cause the loss of 15kt for this year. **..or other potential sources of reduced availability** But this month, the usual outages represent small beer. Instead, we have had to look to other areas for any possible tightness in supply, and one such would be exports of copper and downstream products from Russia. Last December, the Russian government re-introduced an export tax on cathode in order to recoup some additional revenue from high metals prices. Exports of both cathode and wire rod were down last year on 2009 by 4.8% (to 443.6kt) and by 12.8% (to 183.4kt), respectively. The pattern in the past following the introduction of export taxes on refined copper has been for the cathode to be processed into wire rod domestically, and exports of copper units to leave the country that way, duty-free. This trend has indeed continued into January this year, with total refined exports of 11.4kt down heavily _vs._ the 43.2kt seen 12 months ago. Interestingly, Russian apparent refined consumption increased substantially last year, from 389kt to 460kt even though the new export duty was not introduced until year end. It thus appears that refined cathode and wire rod consumption both increased last year, indicating that the rod was processed even further into wire. In Europe at least, to where most cathode and rod are typically exported, there are no reports of excessive Russian material in the market (see Consumption). And this no doubt explains why premia in Europe have remained firm this month. Arguably, the lack of Russian material is being plugged as far as possible by plentiful scrap supplies, which are coming through as a result of stronger manufacturing activity (new scrap) and higher metal prices (the cue for merchants to collect old scrap). In the USA, premia are being pushed back up to around the 5.0-5.5c/lb level, reportedly more as a result of high fuel and trucking costs than good demand for metal itself. The competition issue for truck space between metals and other commodities, which surfaced Q2-2010, has not gone away. **Chinese metal stocks and stalled growth create bearish undertones** A bearish undertone is gathering pace from those who are looking at the substantial metal inventories currently held in Chinese bonded warehouses (~600kt) and elsewhere in that country when set against the poor start to the year in terms of domestic consumption. It is certainly true that demand during the first two months of this year has underperformed levels seen during the same period in 2010 (semis output was down by 2.1% year on year). However, for the world’s largest copper consumer the first quarter has always been the weakest period of the year, as

the chart above shows.  And, while there has been an upward trajectory in successive Q1 performance since 2008, we believe that the relative stagnation during Q1 2011 reflects ongoing destocking throughout the consuming chain, exacerbated by the desire by all participants to hold minimal inventories on account of credit restrictions and high copper prices.  This also has further implications for cathode imports because China typically buys far more metal than is required during the first quarter of each year, leading to a sharp rise in consumer-held commercial stocks that are then drawn down over successive quarters.  The desire to do so this year has been significantly dampened by the unfavourable price arbitrage (a result of the large stocks held in bonded warehouses), high prices, credit restrictions etc. which means that proportionately more stock is thus in the hands of traders in these warehouses than would normally be the case. 

**Some of the Chinese warehouse stocks are being held as collateral** It should also be noted that a significant proportion of the copper in Chinese bonded warehouses is held by parties that do not participate in this market.  These illiquid (at least for now) stocks are typically being used as collateral by the likes of Chinese property developers, especially those who have experienced difficulties in securing bank finance or who have been offered high interestbearing loans (financing metal at closer to LIBOR rates plus holding costs being far more attractive).  According to some estimates, over 50% of this bonded warehouse metal is held under such deals.  This means that as demand picks up, so too should imports if a high percentage of the existing stocks are tightly held. 

**We expect Chinese demand to recover strongly in Q2** Another reason why we are less pessimistic than some relates to seasonal factors in China.  The chart also shows that the second quarter has also been on an upward trajectory from one year to the next in terms of copper demand growth, but more importantly, seasonal factors have meant that Q2 has also been significantly higher than Q1, and we believe that this year will be no exception. 

**Rising Chinese premia – Japanese buying as opposed to heightened domestic demand?** It is possible that we are about to see a turning point in the ongoing rise in Chinese inventories – although we believe that this will come as a result of Japan’s unfortunate circumstances as opposed to higher domestic demand.  Last month, we reported that local cathode sales were running at a discount in RMB terms _vs._ the SHFE price, while imported cathode premia were down to just US$20/t.  Now we understand that the latter have picked up to between US$100-110/t.  Equally, the former – which began the month with a discount of between RMB 280-420/t – saw out March trading at a premium of between RMB30160/t.  It appears that Japanese trading houses have been buying metal from Chinese bonded warehouses (and from Chile)

to cover off any shortfalls of cathode from their own national refineries and to lay the grounds for post-tsunami regional recovery and repair.  Such trade will become more visible in April’s trade statistics, and whether it will be sufficient to reduce market concerns over the build-up in bonded warehouse stocks has yet to be seen.  However, we believe that this will put some upward pressure on Chinese buyers to secure sufficient material for domestic requirements over the forthcoming quarter.  In this light, we still expect Q2 and Q3 cash copper prices to average US$10,000/t ($4.54/lb).

Copper Monthly Update 

## Consumption 

With winter now officially behind us, the warmer spring air is refreshing spirits, although to say that global demand has spring in its step would be an exaggeration.  While activity in Europe has maintained its solid pace of last year, the same cannot be said of the key market China, with semis production lower in the first few months of 2011.  Activity in the US is a little better and while Japan also got off to a steady start, clearly there are short term troubles ahead for the country. We are however, not overly optimistic on the prospects for reconstruction efforts in Japan to boost demand for copper over the medium term. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**Economic activity to slow through 2011** Leading indicators suggest that solid growth in Europe will continue through early 2011, especially in Germany and other Northern European economies.  However, we expect industrial expansion to lose significant momentum by mid-year, as the effects of fiscal contraction begin to kick in and the chance of monetary tightening rises in response to inflationary pressures.  We forecast growth in euro zone industrial output this year of just 2.6%.  That Germany’s industrial output expanded by 12.4% in January, while in Italy IP was higher by just 0.9% illustrates the differences in activity levels across the region. 

**European demand stays in top gear** The European copper market continues to defy expectations of a slowdown in activity, with semis producers reporting continued strong demand for their products.  This is translating into solid refined demand, although some of this is being met by the continued abundance of scrap in the region.  Meanwhile, there has been a dearth of spot purchasing of cathode, perhaps as a result of cathode consumers purchasing on longer term contracts amid fear of product unavailability amid forecasts of a market deficit this year. 

**Rod production exceeding expectations** The wire rod market in Europe continues to perform well, with bookings and output maintaining a healthy clip despite expectations of a slowdown this year.  Given an expected softening in economic and industrial activity this year, in addition to fears of a flood of Russian rod, market players were looking for production levels to be at or slightly above last year

.  However, producers report that they are not seeing much Russian wire rod in Europe and save for the cut back at Elektrokoppar, which we discussed last month, rod mills are reporting that production is up by as much as 10% in the first part of the year. 

**Green means go for copper** Rod makers cite green applications as being behind strong growth in demand for wire rod, with wind turbines a key growth sector because of their high consumption of copper.  We estimate that power generation capacity from wind farms will increase by 8-10% this year, representing around 50kt of copper.  While this is not an insignificant amount on its own, the increasing number of wind farms, in addition to solar farms, is leading to the localisation of the power grid, which is further increasing demand for copper in electricity sub-stations. 

**Mixed picture of European automakers** European car sales fell in February from the prior month, although the yearon-year comparison did at least register an expansion, up by 1.0%, but this still wasn’t sufficient to drag year-to-date sales into positive territory.  The picture across Europe is distinctly mixed, with sales in Germany performing strongly but those in Italy down by a fifth so far this year.  The picture for production is equally cloudy, although strong production in Germany will support demand because of the higher copper intensity of vehicles produced there. 

**Madeco to up Nexans stake to 20%** Chilean semis producer Madeco has agreed to raise its stake in French cable maker Nexans from 9% currently to 20% in a move welcomed by Nexans as its current disparate shareholdings could have left it susceptible to a takeover.  Meanwhile, Nexans will lose its position as the world’s largest cable maker following the takeover of Draka by Italy’s Prysmian. 

**Low single-digit expansion for Western European demand** Despite the strong start to the year for semis production, we continue to expect that demand will moderate in the second half.  As such, we expect European refined demand growth of 2-3% in 2011. 

### **Americas** 

**Mixed set of macro-economic data muddy the demand waters** As always seems to be the case with US macroeconomic data, we have seen a mixed bag of results this month that bode well for the general health of the country on one hand and yet could easily take forward-looking metals demand in the opposite direction.  Economic growth for the 4th quarter of last year was revised upwards this month, from the 2.8% previously noted to 3.1% now.  This was accompanied by a 4% increase in consumer spending over the same period, the strongest quarter for four years.  No doubt seasonal Christmas and New Year consumer purchases were behind this growth.  But in addition there was higher re-stocking of goods by companies who were also buying more plant and equipment.  However, February industrial production fell by 0.1%, and new orders for US manufactured goods also declined unexpectedly.  US durable goods o

rders also fell by 0.9% in February.  The result was well below economist expectations of a 1.1% rise, following the upward correction to January’s result, which was revised to a gain of 3.6% from an initial 2.7%.

**Construction still the drawback for US copper demand...** More specifically for copper, US new home sales fell 16.9% to a 250,000 unit annual pace - the lowest in records going back 48 years and well below analyst expectations which centred on a rise.  The supply of new homes available for sale rose to 8.9 months supply.  The sickly housing market is what has been holding back the US economy.  But there is even some encouragement here, as residential construction grew at an annual rate of 3.3% in the final quarter after falling by over 27% in the prior quarter compared with the same period of 2009.  Furthermore, applications for building permits rose by 7.5% during 2010, higher than expected.  While this is by no means an indication that the construction sector – which accounts for 40% of US copper demand - is back on its feet, what we are detecting, during this climate of low house sales prices in many leading markets, is more activity in the “improvement and repair” segment of existing homes.  With the headline unemployment rate falling to around 9% (even if the long term under- and unemployed remains at closer to 17%), those who can hang onto their homes during this period of negative equity are deciding more so to fix up their homes. 

**...but Mueller Industries believes 2011 will see better times** The tube sector remains the critical drag on semis production and shipments, given the lacklustre construction market.  Domestic shipments remained depressed, down by 3.7% at 256kt for the year to November, according to data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS), but even here the market held up better than expected into the final quarter.  Even so, tube producer Mueller Industries underlined how bad the housing sector was in its 2010 report.  In terms of housing starts, 2009 and 2010 were the two worst years since records began in 1959.  Furthermore, non-residential construction, which declined by 15% in 2009, fell a further 25% in 2010.   But the company believes that both residential and commercial construction markets are stabilising, and will improve throughout this year. 

**China’s Hunan Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube invests in AL** Mueller’s mills in North America, Mexico, the UK and China shipped almost 190kt of copper products last year, 8.1% up on 2009, with the improvements coming in sales to the automotive, industrial and manufacturing OEM sectors.  But it might have more competition from late-2012 in North America at least, now that China’s Hunan Golden Dragon Precise Copper Tube Group has finally committed to a US$100M new plant investment at Thomasville, AL.  Late-March, Golden Dragon and Alabama government

officials held a public meeting to confirm the construction of the plant, which will build copper tubing for plumbing, air condition and the automotive sectors. Golden Dragon, based in Xinxiang, already operates five manufacturing facilities in China spanning high-precision plain copper tube (220kt/a capacity), inner-groove tube (150kt/a), water tube (40kt/a), flat coiled tube (10kt/a) and high efficiency finned tube (10kt/a), and claims to make 15% of all refrigeration and air conditioning copper tubing used worldwide. **Improvement in copper consumption expected this year** We anticipate some further gains in US copper demand this year after 2010’s c.6% gain, albeit at a somewhat limited level of 2.5-3%. This is much improved, though, on the near 1% contraction in demand that we had pencilled in for 2011 only a few months ago, and this is due to the more positive economic environment. Leading this growth will be rod production, which improved almost 10% last year to 1.26Mt. Apparent rod consumption increased by 5.9% last year, according to the ABMS, which was the first year of growth in four. But healthy domestic output was not the sole contributor to this statistic, as weaker imports (down 6.8%) combined with stronger exports (up by 27.8%) to tip the net trade balance in US rod producers’ favour. #### **US copper wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - March 2011 Page 7 of 23 Copper Monthly Update ### **China** **Chinese inflation comes off the boil but only to a simmer** The latest figures for inflation, although still at 4.9% y-o-y in February, at least suggested that price rises are stabilising, while core prices even slowed on the prior month. Arguably, the better news came in the shape of industrial production data, which revealed 14.1% growth in the first two months of the year, up from the 13.5% pace of December and suggesting that recent measures to tame inflation are not unduly crimping industrial and economic activity. Meanwhile, new loans were also less than expected, underlining the impact that China’s tightening measures are having on the economy. **March pick up but sluggish first quarter** Although the order books of most fabricators started to improve in March compared with the sluggish activity in the first two months of the year, production rates are lower than expected. Underlying demand at end users is reasonable enough but high copper prices, in addition to increasing labour, raw material and financing costs have forced end users to maintain inventories at as low levels as possible. Against this backdrop, semis producers a

re becoming increasingly cautious about the outlook for the first half of the year. 

**Data points to mild stock build** We typically see a major stock build in the first quarter of the year as semis producers, and, in fact, the whole supply chain rebuild inventories that were depleted in the final part of the year.  While recent data points to a similar pattern in the first two months of the year, the reasons seem to be different this year.  According to our calculations of CNIA data, apparent consumption of refined copper was flat in the January to February period, despite an increase in SHFE stocks, although semis production was down by 2.1% in the first two months of the year.  This points to a build-up in stocks, although not because of strong apparent refined demand but because of contracting semis output. Meanwhile, we understand that material in bonded warehouses increased further this month, to around 600kt.  While a stock build in the first quarter is not a cause for concern given the sharp increase in demand that normally follows in Q2, the tightening measures ongoing in China and a still fragile global economy make the second quarter the key period in our demand, and, indeed, price forecasts this year.  As such, we discuss this further in the _market developments_ section. 

**Mixed picture for wire rod producers** While demand for fine wire used in automobiles, 3G mobile and high speed trains continues at quite a pace, consumption of magnet wire for home electrical appliances is softer than this time a year ago.  With power cable and building wire also at a more muted pace than last year, some major wire rod makers have lowered production targets for this year and many new lines commissioned in 2010 are running below full capacity.  This is leading to a situation of paper thin profit margins at wire rod producers.  Meanwhile, the narrowing scrap spread is leading to Chinese up casting wire rod mills reducing or even halting production in some cases. 

**Sheet and strip lower overall…** Lead frame strip for high end IC recovered strongly after the Chinese New Year, but some steel strip has replaced copper strip for low end production.  Connector strip demand in March increased by around 15-20% from the low production rate in February, which was mainly driven by the pick up of auto and home electrical appliance production.  The demand of connectors for auto, 3G mobile, and LED products remains very strong. However, bookings for connectors for normal electrical and electronic products are performing less well.  Overall, current production levels at most sheet and strip makers are lower than the first quarter of last year. 

**…but ACR tube hotting up** With the northern hemisphere winter now officially behind us, air conditioner producers are now gearing up for increased production in the coming months.  Indeed, this is driving strong demand in the ACR tube market, with this possibly the strongest end use market at the moment. 

**Auto

production maintains its pace** Latest data for auto sales and production confirm continued momentum in the motor vehicle market despite expectations of a slowdown. Total vehicle production rose by 4.5% year on year, although this was sharply lower on the prior month given the interruption of the Chinese New Year. Taking January and February together, production was up by 8.8% on the first two months of 2010. Motor vehicle sales mirrored production data, with total sales higher by 9.7% in the January to February period. The year-to-date growth rates for both production and sales are broadly in line with our expectations of production growth of around 10% this year. **Demand estimate maintained** While some of the discussion above might initially point to a relatively sluggish year for demand in 2011, in our view developments are in line with our 6% growth estimate for refined copper, which we have left unchanged from last month. l activity.  We were expecting a slowdown in IP in the first and second quarters of the year in any case as base effects from the strong uplift in demand this time last year are worked out of comparisons.  While the effect on first quarter activity from the disaster will be minimal given that it occurred mid-way through March, we expect significant disruption to both GDP and IP in the second quarter of the year, before industrial output stabilises and then picks up towards the year end. 

Manufacturing has faced major disruption from the earthquake and tsunami, initially as a result of the disaster itself and then in the days that followed because of power restrictions.  We are now in a situation where we are seeing logistical and supply chain problems as firms which were unaffected by the disaster itself face difficulty in sourcing components from companies that were.  While there should be sufficient alternative power supply on line by the end of April to meet

demand, there is a distinct possibility of power shortages in the peak summer months as everyone cranks up their air conditioners to beat the stifling heat and humidity. 

**Semis producers suspend operations** We discuss the impact on refined production elsewhere in this report but the key message is that there have been near-term disruptions to smelters and refineries.  Unsurprisingly, the same is also true of the downstream semis sector, with operations at major producers and consumers of semis currently suspended including Hitachi Cable’s five plants in Ibaraki.  While the plants seem to have suffered no structural damage, the plants are suspended because of the absence of power and water supplies. 

**Japanese firms look abroad for cathode** Although some semis producers have suspended operations as a result of power and other issues, there are many other players that are unaffected by the disaster.  It would actually appear that some firms have even looked overseas to source cathode given that several refineries remain closed.  Indeed, we understand that Japanese traders have been purchasing cathode from China and this has helped to pull up premiums from rock bottom levels. 

**Calm before storm for semis shipments** As we note above, we expect semis shipments and output to experience some disruption in the coming months, although in February wire and cable shipments posted an estimated 5.4% year on year growth.  This comes on the back of similar growth in January and is even more impressive given that it compares against a relatively strong upturn at the start of 2010.  However, the very near term outlook for wire and cable shipments in particular is pretty bleak given the closure noted above at Hitachi Cable’s plants. 

**Construction to recover only cautiously** The construction market in Japan has been enjoying something of a mild upturn since the middle of 2010 and housing starts actu

ally rose by 3.1% in 2010 to 813k units. Meanwhile, there is now talk of the re-build related to the earthquake and tsunami driving demand amid a “massive” reconstruction effort. It is easy to overestimate the scale of boost that this will have. We have heard estimates that half a million people have been displaced by the disaster and given that the area devastated was largely rural, many of these people will have lived in houses rather than apartments. As such, it wouldn’t be unreasonable to assume that if around four people live in each house then approximately 125k houses will need to be rebuilt. But because of capacity constraints, these houses will not be built all the same time, and their construction will likely be spread over perhaps as much as three years. In this case, this would only add approximately 5% to housing starts over each of the next few years. However, this of course assumes that all of the houses will be re-built, which may not be the case given fear of returning to the disaster zone. **Autos still only in low gear** A faster upturn in auto production is more likely than in the construction sector, although here too the outlook is still far from clear. A significant number of cars will have been lost during the tsunami which will need to be replaced. At this stage though, many producers are still in production suspensions, with an estimated 300,000 in production losses so far stemming from the shutdowns. As producers battle first with power rationing and then with supply chain and logistical issues a rapid acceleration in production seems unlikely. For the year as a whole we do expect an expansion though, with an upturn of 2-4% estimated. The bad news for copper, however, is that there will have been a significant amount of scrap generated from the cars written off in the tsunami and this should serve to temper optimism about refined copper’s prospects in Japan this year and next. **Demand to contract in 2011** The discussion above sets the scene for a decline in refined copper demand this year and we anticipate a contraction of 1.4%. However, at this stage the near term outlook is still clouded by significant uncertainty. As such, on balance, the risks to this estimate are weighed heavily towards the downside. **China’s February concentrate imports down by almost 30% on a year earlier** Following January’s year-on-year decline in copper concentrate imports, official Chinese statistics show that February fared even worse with receipts down by 29.8%.  This brings the cumulative two-month total to 969.3kdmt compared with 985.8kdmt last year.  Big reductions were recorded in Chilean imports (-33.6% to 265kt) and also those from Peru (-27.9% to 120kt) while receipts from Laos doubled to 62kt.  Given the ongoing growth in Chinese smelting capacity it has come as somewhat of a surprise to many that the country has not been anything like as prominent in the custom concentrate market of late.  Indeed, Chinese spot purchases all but dried up in the second half of last year with the country only now showing some interest because of the sharp rise in terms.  The official statistics for 2010 offer no real guidance as to why this should be as one is able to construct a relatively level concentrate supply/demand balance for last year on the assumption that all of the country’s raw material imports were consumed.  That said the anecdotal evidence points to a materially different outcome with many smelters having accumulated significant concentrate stocks during 2010, with inventories at various plants still at reasonably comfortable levels. 

**Sizeable concentrate surplus in Chinese market last year** Below is an analysis that is based upon official CNIA data. This shows the make up of refined production from primary and secondary sources.  We have removed imported blister from the CNIA secondary production data as this appears to be included in these statisti

cs.  We have then compared the primary refined production figures with the various components that make up this number, i.e. from domestic and imported concentrates, SxEw and imported blister and matte.  Note that these figures are shown on a recoverable basis (i.e. net of 3.4% overall smelting losses where appropriate).  This comparison allows us to calculate an implied stock change for each year.  What this shows is that there has been an implied stock drawdown in each year from 2007 to 2009 and a modest stock build in 2010.  A drawdown of this magnitude (the implied cumulative stock build during the three years to 2009 is 458kt Cu) is not realistic, nor is the very modest stock build in 2010.  If we take the average stock drawdown between 2007 and 2009 plus an allowance for maintaining normal stocks in this growing market and express these as a percentage of the average refined production over the same period we might infer that the statistics are missing the equivalent of 4.5% of refined production feed in each year.  This missing feed is most likely to be from secondary sources, such as unreported scrap, and domestically-produced reverts and by-products from zinc, lead and nickel smelting (cakes, speiss, matte, dross etc.)  If we then apply this unreported feed factor (4.5% of refined production) this allows us to determine a more plausible stock change for each year.

**Global concentrate market in “surplus” last year** Given the implied concentrate stock build in China last year this means that the global concentrate market was in “surplus” by an estimated 170kt Cu in 2010.  This is rather unusual in the context of the ongoing low level of overall primary smelter utilisation rates which remain well below historical norm (i.e. 81% in 2010 compared with optimal levels of closer to 88%).  This might suggest that China is becoming much more sophisticated in the manner in which it operates within the custom concentrate market.  This may in part

be true but it is also apparent that rising smelter operating costs and an unfavourable metal price arbitrage that prevailed for much of last year meant that, for Chinese buyers, spot concentrate purchases were unviable thereby compelling them to seek alternative, more profitable feed sources (i.e. scrap and blister). Scrap is currently in abundant supply in most markets and discounts remain very attractive to buyers. While Chinese smelters will no doubt capitalise on this situation, they also now have a window of opportunity to acquire spot concentrates at far more attractive TC/RCs than has been the case for many years. The much-anticipated re-emergence of China as a major buyer of spot copper concentrates at some point later this year may not now occur due to the combination of these prevailing factors. ## Production news 

**Slight changes only to Japanese refinery output at this stage** Following the earthquake and tsunami disasters in Japan, at this stage we have only made slight changes to our refined production profiles based largely on known conditions at the individual plants themselves.  Overall, we have reduced refined output from Japan for this by under 50kt, to 1.442Mt.  The Onahama smelter-refinery complex, with Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Dowa Metals and Mining and Furukawa Metals & Resources Co as main shareholders, remains closed given that the plant is only 60km from the Fukushima nuclear plant.  While the Onahama port itself has been reopened, there is no news on the condition of the smelter's own wharves.   For the time being, we have reduced the refinery’s output from our former 2011 forecast of 215kt to 180kt, but this could be cut further depending on the operating condition of the plant when workers were told to leave.  Elsewhere, we have cut our forecast output by marginal figures of 5kt or so for Saganoseki and Tamano, given that these were operating below capacity previously due to a shortage of concentrates, and this can be corrected to some degree by re-shipping feed from any idled facilities assuming port congestion is not a major issue. 

**Codelco already downgrades 2011 forecast output** The ongoing issues at its Minera Gaby division have already brought slight revisions to Codelco’s forecast mine output for this year.  As we noted in our January report, Codelco expected to produce 1.8Mt of commercial copper in 2011, but the company is now considering between 1.75-1.78Mt as a more feasible target.  This quarter two particular issues have held back production at the Gabriela Mistral crushing station and SxEw plant, and these have prompted us to reduce our forecast output for this year by 20kt since our February report, to 145kt.  Gaby had already endured a difficult 2010 which saw output fall by almost 21% on 2009 to 117kt.  The division came into production in 2008 and saw 68kt of SxEw copper produced in its first year.  It is designed currently to reach maximum output of 165kt/a during 2012-2013 before levelling out at 120kt/a between 2016-2021. Elsewhere in the Codelco stable, the Las Ventanas smelter is back on line after a planned maintenance programme which became extended by a couple of days following an unauthorised gas emission upon re-start.  We expect Las Ventanas, which can treat in excess of 410k dmt/a concentrate, to produce c.115kt anode this year, largely in line with 2010.
